images.chapterTitle: Chapter उन्नीस — कृष्ण द्वारा मुञ्जारण्य में महाग्नि से रक्षा
images.prompt: Krishna and Balarama walk through the dense Munjavaranya forest with a large group of young cowherds and cattle, surrounded by tall reeds and forest trees. Suddenly, massive wildfire erupts on all sides, with tall orange and red flames spreading rapidly through the dry forest. The cowherds — young boys with sticks and simple clothing — freeze in panic, their faces showing terror, while the cattle huddle together restlessly. Balarama stands nearby, his white complexion stark against the orange glow of the encroaching flames.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Chapter 19

दावाग्निना दह्यमानास्त्रासिताः शरणं गताः ।
कृष्णं विविशुः सर्वे नेत्रे उन्मील्य विस्मिताः ॥

"Scorched by the wildfire and overwhelmed with fear, they all took shelter of Krishna — and opening their eyes, they were filled with wonder."

One afternoon, Krishna and Balarama led their beloved cowherd friends and cattle deep into the Munjavaranya — the forest of tall munja reeds. The boys wandered freely, laughing and playing, unaware of the danger hiding in the dry undergrowth.

Without warning, a massive wildfire erupted on all sides. Walls of roaring flame rose up, devouring the reeds and trees, sealing every path of escape. The young boys froze in terror — their faces pale, their feet rooted to the ground. The cattle pressed together, trembling. Even Balarama, radiant and powerful, stood watching as the inferno tightened its ring around them.

With nowhere to run, the frightened boys cried out — "Krishna! Save us!"

Krishna smiled. He asked them to close their eyes and have no fear. They obeyed — and in a single breath, Krishna swallowed the entire wildfire whole. When the boys opened their eyes, they stood safely in an open meadow, the forest peaceful and unburned.

When the world becomes a wall of flames, the devotee's only shelter is Krishna — who swallows our fears as effortlessly as a breath.

🙏 Hare Krishna

images.chapterTitle: Chapter उन्नीस — कृष्ण द्वारा मुञ्जारण्य में महाग्नि से रक्षा
images.prompt: The terrified cowherds rush toward Krishna, falling at his feet with joined hands, their faces pale with fear as flames close in around the forest clearing. Krishna stands calm and reassuring among them, his dark blue skin glowing gently, gesturing to all the frightened boys and Balarama to close their eyes. The cattle stand trembling behind the boys, the roaring fire visible in a ring around the entire group in the Munjavaranya forest.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Chapter 19

"मीलयध्वं दृशः सर्वे मा भैष्ट व्रजवासिनः"

"Close your eyes, all of you — fear not, O residents of Vraja."

The boys of Vrindavan had wandered deep into the Munjavaranya forest with their cattle, lost in the joy of play — unaware that a ring of wildfire was silently tightening around them.

When the roaring flames finally appeared on all sides, panic swept through the cowherd boys. Smoke filled the air. The cattle trembled and pressed together. The boys ran — not away, but toward Krishna, falling at His feet with folded hands, their faces pale, their voices trembling: "Krishna! Save us!"

And Krishna — blue as a monsoon cloud, utterly still — looked upon them with eyes full of love and calm certainty. He asked only one thing of them: "Close your eyes. Trust Me."

They did. Every boy, Balarama, every frightened calf — eyes shut, hearts surrendered.

In that moment of total faith, Krishna swallowed the entire forest fire — consuming it completely, leaving no ash, no ember, no trace. When they opened their eyes, they stood safe in an open meadow.

This is the miracle of surrender — not escape from danger, but the closing of eyes in complete trust, while Krishna does what only He can do.

🙏 Hare Krishna

images.chapterTitle: Chapter उन्नीस — कृष्ण द्वारा मुञ्जारण्य में महाग्नि से रक्षा
images.prompt: Krishna stands alone at the center of the forest clearing, tilting his head back with mouth wide open, as the enormous blazing wildfire is visibly drawn inward and swallowed into his mouth — streams of flame flowing toward him like a river reversing course. The cowherds and Balarama stand behind him with eyes just opening, their expressions shifting from fear to awe and wonder. The forest is now completely calm, cool, and unburned around them, cattle standing peacefully.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Chapter 19

मुखे निधाय तां वह्निं निद्राणानबोधयत् ।
तं तथाभूतमालक्ष्य गोपा मेनिरे दिवौकसम् ॥

"Placing that fire into His mouth, Krishna then awakened the sleeping cowherd boys. Seeing Him in this wondrous state, the gopas concluded that He must be a divine being."

Deep in the Muñjāraṇya forest, a raging wildfire had erupted without warning — walls of flame roaring through the dry thickets, encircling the exhausted cowherd boys and their cattle. In sheer terror, they cried out: "Krishna! Balarama! Save us!"

Krishna told them simply: "Close your eyes. Do not be afraid."

They obeyed. And then — the impossible happened.

Krishna tilted His head back, opened His mouth, and drew the entire blazing inferno inward — rivers of fire reversing course, streaming into Him like the ocean swallowing a wave. The roar of flames became silence. The scorching heat became cool forest air.

When the boys opened their eyes, every tree stood untouched. Every cow grazed peacefully. The forest was whole, as if fire had never come. And there stood Krishna — smiling gently, as though nothing had happened.

Balarama and the gopas stared in stunned, trembling awe. Who is this boy? Surely no ordinary child walks among us.

When the fires of our own lives consume us with fear, He is already drawing them into Himself. We need only close our eyes and trust.

🙏 Hare Krishna

images.chapterTitle: अध्याय में आगे चलकर वरुण कहते हैं—अजानता मामकेन मूढेन—मेरे अज्ञानी नौकर ने यह किया
images.prompt: Varuna, the divine god of waters, sits on his celestial throne in his underwater palace surrounded by flowing currents and sea creatures, speaking with a humble and apologetic expression, raising one hand in explanation while his attendants bow nearby. He addresses an unseen presence, his face showing remorse as he explains that an ignorant servant of his committed an unintended act without knowledge.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 6, Chapter 170

अजानता मामकेन मूढेन कृतमप्रियम्

"This unpleasant act was done by my ignorant and foolish servant, who did not know better."

In the golden depths of his celestial underwater palace, where luminous currents swirl and sea creatures bow in reverence, Lord Varuṇa — the great god of waters and cosmic order — sits upon his divine throne with an expression of deep remorse.

A grave mistake has been made. One of Varuṇa's servants, acting in ignorance, committed an offense against an innocent soul — an act never sanctioned by the lord himself. Now Varuṇa, rather than deflecting blame, raises his hand with honesty and humility, openly declaring: *this was done by my foolish servant who did not understand.*

This moment is profound — a powerful celestial lord taking moral accountability, not hiding behind his authority. He does not punish his servant silently. He faces the wronged party with transparency and seeks forgiveness.

In our own lives, how often do we deflect blame rather than own the mistakes within our sphere? Varuṇa teaches us that true greatness lies in humble acknowledgment — of our ignorance, and of those under our care.

🙏 Hare Krishna

images.chapterTitle: अध्याय में आगे चलकर वरुण कहते हैं—अजानता मामकेन मूढेन—मेरे अज्ञानी नौकर ने यह किया
images.prompt: Varuna's unnamed ignorant servant stands before his master in an underwater or riverside setting, head bowed in shame and remorse, hands folded, dressed in simple attendant's garments. Varuna towers above him with a stern yet measured expression, the word 'mūḍha' (foolish one) hanging in the air as aquatic life and flowing water surround the scene, symbolizing the servant's unwitting transgression.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 6, Chapter 17

अजानता मामकेन मूढेन कृतमीदृशम्

"This was done by my foolish servant who did not know what he was doing."

Beneath the sacred waters, where aquatic life moves in silent witness, a trembling servant stands before the mighty Lord Varuṇa — head bowed, hands folded, robes of a simple attendant upon his shamed frame.

This servant, unnamed yet unforgotten, had overstepped — seizing or obstructing what was not his to touch, unaware of the divine order he disturbed.

Varuṇa, lord of the cosmic waters and upholder of divine law, does not rage. Instead, he does something rare among the powerful — he owns the fault of his own household.

"Mūḍha," he says — 'this foolish one' — acknowledging ignorance, not malice, as the root.

In this moment, the scene teaches us: true authority is not blind loyalty to one's servants' wrongs. A great master names the error, separates intent from action, and seeks rectification with dignity.

The flowing waters around them carry away both guilt and pride — leaving only truth.

When those under our care err unknowingly, may we have Varuṇa's grace — to correct with honesty, not cover with silence.

🙏 Hare Krishna

images.chapterTitle: अध्याय में आगे चलकर वरुण कहते हैं—अजानता मामकेन मूढेन—मेरे अज्ञानी नौकर ने यह किया
images.prompt: Varuna stands with open palms in a gesture of honest confession and accountability, his majestic form draped in blue and white robes with a water-crown, speaking the Sanskrit words 'ajānatā māmakena mūḍhena' — acknowledging that the act was done by his own ignorant one. A divine light surrounds the scene as Varuna takes moral responsibility, embodying the divine virtue of honest acknowledgment of one's servant's fault.
images.caption:
📖 Srimad Bhagavatam — Canto 6, Chapter 17

अजानता मामकेन मूढेन अपराधः कृतः प्रभो

"O Lord, this offense was committed by my ignorant servant who did not know."

In this profound moment, the mighty Lord Varuṇa — god of the cosmic waters and divine law — stands before Nārada Muni with open palms, his blue and white robes shimmering, his water-crown gleaming in divine light.

What had happened? Varuṇa's servant, acting without knowledge, had wrongfully seized Nārada's disciple Citraketu — a grave transgression against a great sage and devotee of the Lord.

Rather than deflect or deny, Varuṇa does something extraordinary: he openly confesses. He names the fault clearly — *ajānatā*, done without knowledge; *mūḍhena*, by a foolish one. He takes accountability as the master, even for another's error.

This is the dharma of a true leader — not to hide behind position, but to stand in truth with humility.

In a world quick to blame others and slow to acknowledge wrongs, Varuṇa's words carry timeless wisdom: real nobility is seen not in power, but in the courage to say — *this wrong happened under my care, and I own it.*

May we carry this same honest accountability into our own lives and relationships.

🙏 Hare Krishna
